Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time — we'll go through the iteration three numbers we ran this week, uh quick round-robin intros?
[00:12] Priya Patel: Priya, head of MLOps at Auralis. thanks.
[00:16] Markus Eriksen: Markus, CTO.
[00:19] Janelle Cruz: Janelle, platform.
[00:21] Ben Thornton: Ben, data science.
[00:23] Sofia Martinez: great. Ethan, you want to kick with the topline?
[00:26] Ethan Walker: yeah, sure. so quick disclaimer, the numbers are from our lab harness — synthetic replay of Auralis prompts, 65% short (<=128), 35% medium (<=512), peak conc 90 concurrent. we compared Redwood Dedicated config (q4 quant, 2xA100) against Auralis' baseline provider that they shared — vendor X setup, single region.
[00:48] Ethan Walker: Topline: p50 latency down ~22% vs baseline for the default chat model variant, p95 improved ~17%. throughput sustained at 640 rps vs baseline 420 rps for identical sequence mix. cost per 1M tokens estimated 14% lower after batching gains.
[01:10] Priya Patel: sorry can you repeat the cost bit? I missed that.
[01:13] Ethan Walker: yeah, so after applying continuous batching and prefix kv-cache, our estimate for normalized cost per one million tokens is about 14% lower than your baseline, assuming similar tokenization and no extra third-party egress. There's a caveat — that number depends on hit rates for the cache.
[01:27] Ben Thornton: what's the p95 numbers again?
[01:29] Ethan Walker: p95 was 480 ms on Redwood Dedicated, baseline was ~580 ms. p50 about 78 ms vs 100 ms baseline.
[01:36] Markus Eriksen: those are promising, but our SLO is 200 ms p95 for the user flows we care about. how confident are you these hold under the longer seq lengths we saw in prod? we have a tail of 2048 tokens on 8% of requests.
[01:51] Sofia Martinez: good question — the current runs mostly used max seq 512. for the 2048 tail, we ran a small stress sample and saw p95 climb to 1.1s, but throughput drop is expected; Ethan has a tuning plan that helps keep p95 nearer to your SLO by using dynamic kernel selection and partial kv-cache priming.
[02:08] Ethan Walker: yeah, so recommended: enable kv-cache warmup for sessions that exceed 512, use variable batch timeouts to avoid head-of-line blocking, and consider a hybrid: keep short/medium interactions on hosted low-latency pool and route long sequences to dedicated capacity where cost efficiency is better.
[02:26] Janelle Cruz: can you explain the kv-cache warmup — is that something we need to instrument in our client?
[02:31] Ethan Walker: it's a server-side option we can enable in the runtime; it preloads common prefixes and reuses hidden state where session continuity is present. minimal client changes: just propagate session-id header. there was a note in the doc — we sent a short note last week.
[02:45] Priya Patel: on cost, what's the delta if we enable 8-bit quant vs q4 quant? our compliance team is wary of any quality regressions.
[02:53] Ethan Walker: good point. q4 gave the best perf/cost trade in our tests with negligible quality diffs on your eval set. 8-bit (int8) adds more cost saving, roughly another 6–9% but with slightly more hallucination risk on narrow, safety-sensitive prompts — we'd recommend running the eval suite on the dev cluster to validate.
[03:12] Ben Thornton: did you run the evals on our actual prompt set or synthetic?
[03:16] Ethan Walker: both. we used the synthetic load for throughput and latency, but did a smaller pass of your curated eval prompts for quality metrics. sample size was 1.2k prompts. not huge, so another run is advisable.
[03:26] Markus Eriksen: also, the baseline provider had multi-region mirroring — they keep traffic in region to reduce latency for EU users, are your numbers single-region?
[03:34] Ethan Walker: these runs were single region (us-west). multi-region routing would reduce regional tail by ~30ms typically, and Redwood supports smart routing — we can mirror or route by region per your config.
[03:44] Sofia Martinez: small note — the baseline's numbers were from their managed endpoint w/ autoscale but no dedicated GPUs. that's something to watch when comparing cost because their burst model can look cheaper at low volume.
[03:56] Priya Patel: okay. on compliance — SOC2 and KMS: we need to know where logs land and SOC2 report availability before we can start any dedicated runs.
[04:06] Sofia Martinez: yes — Redwood has SOC2 Type II and we can share the report via the NDA channel. for KMS, we support customer-managed keys in both Redwood Private and Dedicated; on hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK via KMS integrations. I'll add a security deep-dive follow-up to the notes.
[04:22] Janelle Cruz: is Private the same as Dedicated? what's the difference on the infra side?
[04:26] Ethan Walker: short answer: Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity managed by Redwood in our cloud; Private is a deployment model that can include a VPC or on-prem bundle where control plane is separated and you can bring your own infra. Private gives more network isolation, Dedicated gives simplest manageability and still strong isolation.
[04:44] Markus Eriksen: latency-wise, would Private add any overhead vs Dedicated?
[04:48] Ethan Walker: negligible — if it's in the same data center and we optimize kernels similarly. network egress and your internal routing could add ms, but compute path is the same.
[04:57] Ben Thornton: curious about degradation scenarios — if the cluster hits capacity, what fallbacks exist?
[05:02] Ethan Walker: we have policy-based fallbacks: route to a lower-cost model variant, or to cross-region capacity; can also degrade max tokens or apply stricter batching to preserve overall throughput. We'll share sample routing policies.
[05:14] Priya Patel: about the benchmark spreadsheet — can you annotate which rows are synthetic vs real prompts, and include standard deviation columns? makes it easier for our SRE to ingest.
[05:23] Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll annotate. Ethan will trim and push a cleaned CSV.
[05:27] Ethan Walker: noted. also there's a couple of anomalies — a small spike around 11:12 in the run where p95 jumped to 2.6s, looks like a GC event on the harness VM; we flagged those and removed when computing median numbers.
[05:43] Janelle Cruz: for the 2-hour dedicated run you suggested, do you want traffic replay or synthetic fan-out?
[05:49] Ethan Walker: replay is better — replay at 1x traffic pattern you provided, with sequence length distribution preserved. replay helps reveal cache hit-rate impacts.
[05:57] Priya Patel: timeline — if we run the 2-hour test next week and share logs, how fast can you iterate on tuning?
[06:02] Ethan Walker: typically 2–3 business days to process traces and deliver tuned config; if we see large regressions might take longer but we'll prioritise.
[06:10] Sofia Martinez: quick objection that sometimes comes up — what about vendor lock-in if we use Redwood-specific tuning?
[06:14] Ethan Walker: good question — the tuning is mostly parameter-level (batch-size, timeout, kv-warmup) and not proprietary, so it's portable. the runtime optimizations are our value-add, but customers can export configs and we document the settings.
[06:28] Markus Eriksen: any rough SLA numbers for Dedicated we can see on paper?
[06:32] Sofia Martinez: yes, Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and target latency tiers. I'll send the SLA excerpt.
[06:36] Ben Thornton: can you talk about token billing discrepancies? last time we saw token counts off between providers.
[06:42] Ethan Walker: tokenization differences happen; we normalize on Tiktoken vX in our sheet and include raw token counts per prompt so you can map to your internal meter.
[06:50] Priya Patel: about the p95 at 1.1s for long tails — is there a routing rule you suggest to automatically send >1024 sequences to dedicated to guarantee SLO?
[06:59] Ethan Walker: yes, you can set a routing policy on sequence length and user tier. we recommend a soft route with canary first — send 10% of those long sequences to dedicated then ramp.
[07:10] Priya Patel: ok that helps.
[07:12] Sofia Martinez: any other risks we should surface?
[07:15] Janelle Cruz: network egress cost if we go multi-region, and cross-account KMS setup complexity.
[07:20] Sofia Martinez: we'll include egress estimates in the spreadsheet and a short KMS checklist for your infra team.
[07:27] Ethan Walker: one more note — we saw a ~9% latency improvement if you disable op fusion for certain kernel paths on your long sequences; it's a knob we can flip and benchmark.
[07:37] Ben Thornton: interesting, could you capture that as an experiment?
[07:40] Ethan Walker: yes — we'll add an experiment row labeled "op-fusion-toggle" in the sheet.
[07:45] Sofia Martinez: alright let's do a very quick recap and next steps.
[07:48] Sofia Martinez: 1) Redwood to share trimmed benchmark CSV annotated by synthetic vs real and std-dev (Ethan/Sofia, due 12/04)
[07:56] Sofia Martinez: 2) Auralis to run 2-hour replay in staging (Janelle) and provide logs (due 12/08)

[08:10] Sofia Martinez: 4) Redwood to propose batching + kv-cache config and op-fusion experiment (Ethan, due 12/06)
[08:17] Markus Eriksen: sounds good. one ask — can the CSV include a cost projection for 1M, 10M token volumes and a 12-mo runway for dedicated?
[08:26] Sofia Martinez: yes we'll add cost projection rows and a simple 12-month committed vs on-demand calc.
[08:31] Priya Patel: thanks all. quick note — we'll loop in procurement if numbers look good.
[08:35] Sofia Martinez: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the sheet.
